opus-5.5.text:
Because it changes the shape of the curve. For most of the history of this field, progress has been bottlenecked by people: how many talented researchers you have, how many experiments they can design and run, how quickly they can read the results and decide what to try next. Compute has been growing enormously, but the human loop around it hasn't really sped up.

Once the models get good enough to meaningfully help with that loop, writing the code, running the experiments, debugging the training runs, even proposing ideas, then the thing you're improving is also the thing doing the improving. That's a feedback loop, and feedback loops behave very differently from linear progress.

And honestly, a lot of this work is very well suited to these systems. Much of what an ML researcher does day to day is fairly mechanical: you have a hypothesis, you change some code, you launch a job, you look at a loss curve, you figure out why something blew up. If a model can take on a big chunk of that, each human researcher suddenly has the leverage of a whole team. You go from "we can try ten ideas this month" to "we can try a thousand."

So when I say it's a milestone, I mean it's the point where AI stops being just a product of research and becomes a participant in it. After that, the pace of everything downstream, science, medicine, engineering, can accelerate, because the engine driving the improvement is itself getting better. That's why I think it's one of the most important things to get right, both in terms of capability and in terms of making sure we stay thoughtful about where it's heading.

r001.rationale: It says AI can help with the research loop that improves AI, creating a feedback loop where the system doing the improving also gets better.

r002.rationale: It discusses researchers using models to run experiments, but does not identify model users’ feedback or improving models around what users care about.

r003.rationale: It does not mention global excitement about AI or AI funding as a reinforcing flywheel.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, if you look at what's actually driven progress in this field, it's been a lot of people doing a lot of experiments and getting a lot of things wrong. I mean, the Transformer came out of a bunch of us at Google trying things and throwing most of them away. Mixture of experts, same thing. The ideas are cheap. The expensive part is the iteration: you have an idea, you implement it, you train the thing, you look at the loss curve, you realize you had a bug, you fix it, you run it again. That loop is where the time goes.

So the reason I think AI helping build the next AI is such a big deal is that it's the first time that loop gets a real speedup. Right now the bottleneck is researcher hours. There are only so many people in the world who are good at this, and each of them can only run so many experiments and read so many results in a day. If the models get good enough to do a meaningful fraction of that work, write the kernel, debug the training run, propose the ablation and actually go run it, then you're not scaling progress with headcount anymore. You're scaling it with compute.

And that's a different regime. It compounds. Every improvement you make to the model makes it a slightly better researcher, which gets you the next improvement faster. We've seen little hints of this already. Models are pretty good at writing code now, they're decent at reading papers, they can tell you when your experiment design is dumb. None of that is the whole job yet. But it doesn't have to be the whole job. If it takes thirty percent of the grind off of a good researcher, that's already enormous.

I'll admit I'm also just excited about it personally. I've spent a lot of years staring at TensorBoard. If the model wants to take that part, it can have it.

astra-6.text:
Because it changes the feedback loop. So far, progress in AI has depended on people doing research, writing code, running experiments, and figuring out what worked. If AI can help with those things, then a better model can help us build an even better model.

That doesn’t necessarily mean everything suddenly takes off overnight. You still have constraints like compute and the time it takes to run experiments. But you’re putting more intelligence into the process of improving intelligence. That could make progress much faster, and that’s why it’s such an important milestone.
